record.title: ASEAN scam prevention is not converting into resolution, recovery, or durable digital trust

record.title: Diary-based time use shows care and disability as hidden conversion costs for free time and social life
record.source_unit: Australian Bureau of Statistics, How Australians use their time, 2024; supplementary disability, carer, and time-pressure tables released August 5, 2026
record.geography: Australia; people aged 15 years and over in in-scope private households

observations.period: 2024 Time Use Survey; two diary days per in-scope person; total population averages

denominator.unit: assigned diary days per person for the main survey design; the published tables provide weighted national estimates

free_time_participation.unit: percent participating in free-time activities on a diary day

in_person_socialising_participation.unit: percent talking and socialising in person on a diary day

free_time_average_total_population.unit: hours:minutes average per day across the total population

in_person_socialising_average_total_popu.unit: hours:minutes average per day among people who participated in the activity

observations.method: ABS 2024 Time Use Survey diary estimates; participants recorded activities in five-minute increments for two consecutive days, with weighted national tables reporting participation and average time.
observations.uncertainty: The survey is a snapshot, not a longitudinal panel; one activity is recorded as the main activity at a time, seasonal and day-of-week composition matters, and participation prevalence cannot be inferred from two diary days for infrequent activities.
observations.subgroup: Australian residents aged 15 years and over in scope private households.
observations.counterinterpretation: Free time is a broad category and average time among participants is not the same as time available to every person; socialising can occur simultaneously or outside the diary classification.

observations.period: 2024 Time Use Survey; disability-status supplementary tables

denominator.unit: weighted national population frame for people aged 15 years and over, split by ABS disability status; table reports participation and participant-time averages

in_person_socialising_participation_has_.unit: percent of people with disability participating on a diary day

in_person_socialising_participation_no_d.unit: percent of people without disability participating on a diary day

free_time_average_among_participants_has.unit: hours:minutes average per day among people with disability who participated in free time

free_time_average_among_participants_no_.unit: hours:minutes average per day among people without disability who participated in free time

mechanism.value: Disability does not appear as a simple attendance gap in the diary-day socialising measure, but participant time differs: access, energy, health, transport, and available alternatives may shape the duration and composition of free time after participation occurs

observations.method: ABS Table 11.1 and Table 11.3, participation and average time by disability status, age group, and sex; averages are among participants unless explicitly identified as total-population averages.
observations.uncertainty: Disability is defined as a limitation, restriction, impairment, disease, or disorder lasting or expected to last at least six months and restricting everyday activities; the cross-sectional diary does not identify accessibility barriers or causal effects.
observations.subgroup: Australians aged 15 years and over by ABS disability status; selected age and sex cells are also available.
observations.counterinterpretation: Longer free-time duration among participants with disability may reflect selection into the activity, different schedules, health-related non-work time, or activity classification rather than greater leisure access or wellbeing.

observations.period: 2024 Time Use Survey; carer-status supplementary tables

denominator.unit: weighted national population frame for people aged 15 years and over, split by whether the person reported providing care to another person

caring_support_participation_carers.unit: percent of people who provided care to another person participating in caring and support on a diary day

caring_support_participation_noncarers.unit: percent of people who did not provide care to another person participating in caring and support on a diary day

caring_support_average_among_participant.unit: hours:minutes average per day among carers who participated in caring and support
hours:minutes average per day among non-carers who participated in caring and support

free_time_average_among_participants_car.unit: hours:minutes average per day among carers who participated in free time

free_time_average_among_participants_non.unit: hours:minutes average per day among non-carers who participated in free time

mechanism.value: Care is a hidden time-price route: carers are much more likely to record caring and support on the diary day and spend longer in that activity, while their participant-level free-time average is slightly lower

observations.method: ABS Table 12.1 and Table 12.3, participation and average time by carer status, age group, and sex; carer status is based on the survey question about providing care to another person and diary participation is measured separately.
observations.uncertainty: The survey is not designed to estimate the prevalence of carers from two diary days; care may not occur on an assigned diary day, and participant averages cannot be summed across categories or interpreted as total-population time without the correct universe.
observations.subgroup: Australians aged 15 years and over by reported carer status, with age and sex breakdowns.
observations.counterinterpretation: The small free-time difference among participants does not mean carers experience no time burden; carers may have different schedules, employment, health, household support, or opportunities to participate in free time.

observations.method: Randomized field experiment exploiting exogenous variation in giving agents access to AI-generated response suggestions; the article measures response efficiency and automated sentiment changes across chats.

observations.counterinterpretation: Faster and more empathetic messages can improve the interaction without fixing the underlying delivery or account problem; automated sentiment can also miss frustration, repeat effort, or later switching.

denominator.unit: conversation-type and handoff comparisons within the experiment's customer-service chats; subgroup denominator not stated in the public abstract

observations.method: The study uses customer intent categories and a data feature in which customers first interacted with an automated chatbot before transfer to a human agent who may or may not have AI assistance.

record.title: A large-load operating event moved data-center dependency from forecast risk into grid-response rules

record.title: Undersea cable redundancy is a geopolitical and economic-continuity dependency, not only a bandwidth issue
record.source_unit: U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission contracted research report on China, trans-Pacific cables, vulnerability, and disruption modeling
record.geography: United States, Taiwan, Japan, Philippines, Hawaii, Guam, and trans-Pacific cable networks

observations.period: September 2026 report; strategic capability and gray-zone exposure assessment

denominator.unit: operational trans-Pacific cable systems included in the report's network modeling

fcc_lit_capacity_coverage.unit: percent of trans-Pacific cable capacity accounted for by U.S. operator lit-capacity data

repair_vessels.unit: cable vessels globally, with up to 36 potentially unavailable for repairs at a given time according to the report

china_hmn_new_system_share.unit: percent of new cable systems built between 2020 and 2024 supplied by HMN Technologies

china_hmn_planned_kilometer_share.unit: percent of planned cable kilometers through 2026 attributed to HMN Technologies

observations.method: Descriptive synthesis of the USCC-posted contracted research report's capability review, cable-industry evidence, vulnerability index, and network modeling. The report is presented as research prepared for the Commission's deliberations and is not necessarily endorsed by the Commission or its staff.
observations.uncertainty: The report distinguishes accidental or natural breakages from suspected sabotage but does not establish future attack probability. Industry shares, vessel availability, cable capacity, and network exposure are time-sensitive; some lit-capacity and demand inputs are estimated, and the report's analytical judgments are not observed incidents.
observations.subgroup: Trans-Pacific cable systems, cable operators, repair fleets, U.S.-connected island routes, Chinese undersea technology firms, and U.S. economic users reliant on low-latency connections.
observations.counterinterpretation: China's reduced share of planned cable kilometers may reflect geopolitical exclusion from projects rather than reduced technical capability; cable breakage is usually accidental or natural, and redundancy can improve through capacity upgrades, new routes, repair, and coordination.

observations.period: September 2026; modeled peak-demand residual-capacity scenarios

denominator.unit: illustrative multi-cable disruption scenarios in the report's peak-demand residual-headroom table

top_three_highest_risk_cables.unit: percent residual headroom to lit capacity under peak demand when TPE, PLCN, and NCP are disrupted

top_five_highest_risk_cables.unit: percent residual headroom to lit capacity under peak demand when TPE, PLCN, NCP, AAG, and FASTER are disrupted

taiwan_contingency.unit: percent residual headroom to lit capacity under peak demand when four direct U.S.-Taiwan connections are disrupted

top_two_largest_cables.unit: percent residual headroom to lit capacity under peak demand when JUNO and PLCN are disrupted; negative indicates modeled overload

guam_single_cable_design_headroom.unit: less than percent headroom if one of Guam's two continental-U.S. cables is broken even after maximum-design-capacity upgrades

observations.method: Scenario model using published design capacity for 25 operational trans-Pacific systems, estimated lit capacity, high- and low-stress demand assumptions, and alternative-routing analysis. Peak demand is modeled at 70%-80% of lit capacity; the report separately models latency and average-demand conditions.
observations.uncertainty: This is a scenario exercise, not a forecast or observed outage record. Demand between routes is not publicly observed, some lit capacity is estimated, the network snapshot is primarily current to end-2024, and cable upgrades or repairs could change the result. Negative headroom is modeled overload, not a measured service outage.
observations.subgroup: Trans-Pacific routes linking the United States with Taiwan, Japan, and the Philippines, plus domestic Pacific connections to Hawaii and Guam; downstream users include internet, financial, cloud, AI, and communications services.
observations.counterinterpretation: A modeled capacity shortfall need not become a realized consumer or firm outage if traffic is rerouted, demand is lower, capacity is upgraded, repair fleets respond quickly, or alternative systems enter service.

record.boundary: This record adds an external geopolitical-infrastructure dependency and scenario-model layer. It does not establish Chinese intent, a sabotage event, future attack probability, realized connectivity loss, consumer harm, firm loss, or U.S. strategic leverage; modeled capacity and latency effects must remain separate from observed outages and downstream outcomes.

observations.uncertainty: The measures use different years, populations and definitions; price change is not equivalent to affordability change, and overburden does not capture quality, insecurity or access to nearby services by itself.
observations.subgroup: EU households, urban residents, low-income households and respondents in 27 OECD countries.
observations.counterinterpretation: Aggregate EU housing-cost indicators can conceal major national and regional differences, including places where social housing, rental regulation or household incomes buffer price pressure.

observations.period: 2024–2025; social-economy role in affordable housing

denominator.unit: Housing-stock measures for selected EU member states; country coverage and social-housing definitions vary

social_housing_provider_share_netherland.unit: percent of social rental housing stock provided by social-economy entities in the Netherlands

social_housing_provider_share_austria.unit: percent of social rental housing stock provided by social-economy entities in Austria

social_housing_provider_share_france.unit: percent of social rental housing stock provided by social-economy entities in France

nonprofit_housing_stock_netherlands.unit: approximate share of total housing stock represented by non- or limited-profit organizations in the Netherlands

participatory_delivery.value: Social-economy housing entities combine affordability with service provision, community development and sometimes participatory governance

observations.method: OECD Affordable Housing Database and country examples synthesized in the OECD–EU report.
observations.uncertainty: Social housing definitions differ across countries, and provider share does not directly establish rents, quality, waiting times, resident power or access for the lowest-income households.
observations.subgroup: Selected EU member states and their social-rental and broader housing stocks.
observations.counterinterpretation: Large provider shares may reflect historical institutional arrangements and cannot be transplanted without land, finance, governance and public-capacity conditions.

observations.period: 2025; enabling conditions for social-economy care and housing delivery

denominator.unit: OECD–EU report synthesis; no single respondent or entity denominator

priority_sectors.value: Care and affordable housing are treated as priority areas shaped by ageing, rising housing costs, limited supply and widening inequality

institutional_arrangements.value: Effective delivery depends on arrangements across national, regional and municipal levels

business_support.value: Business-support ecosystems are identified as a framework condition for social-economy expansion

fiscal_measures.value: Taxation and fiscal measures are identified as a framework condition alongside institutional arrangements and business support

care_workforce.value: The report emphasizes quality, accessible care, long-term partnerships and better recognition of care occupations

observations.method: Comparative policy analysis of social-economy care and housing models and their institutional conditions.
observations.uncertainty: The report identifies enabling conditions and examples, not a common impact evaluation or proof that social-economy provision outperforms public or private provision in every setting.
observations.subgroup: National, regional and municipal authorities; social-economy entities; care workers; residents and households needing housing or care.
observations.counterinterpretation: Social-economy organizations can complement but cannot replace public financing, universal standards or sufficient supply; shifting delivery without resources may simply relocate unpaid or underpaid work.

related_sources.claim: Official OECD publication record and DOI for the OECD–European Commission report.
Official downloadable PDF used for retrieval verification and hashing.

record.boundary: This record adds an institutional-delivery mechanism: housing and care affordability pressures create room for non-profit, limited-profit and cooperative organizations to function as locally rooted infrastructure, but their capacity depends on public framework conditions, finance, procurement and accountability. It is comparative policy and administrative evidence, not a universal causal evaluation of the social economy or a substitute for local service-capacity data.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official OECD full report, housing chapter, publication record and PDF were retrieved and reviewed for social-economy scale, housing affordability, provider shares, care and housing delivery mechanisms, and enabling conditions; the PDF was hashed.

record.title: Renewable deployment is accelerating, but technology and regional concentration shape who gains energy security
record.source_unit: International Renewable Energy Agency, Renewable Capacity Statistics 2026
record.geography: Global renewable power generation capacity, with regional and technology comparisons for 2016-2025 and detailed 2025 additions

observations.period: 2025; global renewable capacity expansion

denominator.unit: global renewable power capacity stock and annual additions

total_capacity.unit: GW of total renewable power capacity at end-2025

annual_growth.unit: percent annual increase in renewable capacity

share_of_total_additions.unit: percent of total global power-capacity expansion represented by renewables

observations.method: IRENA compilation of renewable power capacity installed and connected at year end using questionnaires, official national statistics, industry associations, reports, and news sources.
observations.uncertainty: Capacity is maximum net generating capacity, not electricity actually generated; reporting coverage, revisions, grid connection, and source quality vary across countries and technologies.
observations.subgroup: Utilities, governments, grid operators, investors, workers, households, firms, and communities affected by power-system investment and reliability.
observations.counterinterpretation: Rapid capacity growth does not by itself establish affordability, reliability, emissions reductions, access, or equitable local benefits.

observations.period: 2025; technology composition of renewable additions

denominator.unit: GW of renewable capacity added globally in 2025

solar_pv_component.unit: GW of solar photovoltaic capacity within solar additions

solar_wind_share.unit: percent of net renewable additions from solar and wind together

observations.method: IRENA technology-level accounting of annual additions across solar, wind, hydropower, bioenergy, geothermal, and off-grid systems.
observations.uncertainty: Technology shares describe nameplate capacity additions and do not measure dispatchability, storage, capacity factors, lifecycle impacts, or local system integration costs.
observations.subgroup: Solar and wind manufacturers, miners and material suppliers, grid planners, energy workers, consumers, and communities hosting generation and transmission.
observations.counterinterpretation: Concentration in solar and wind can reflect falling costs and rapid deployment while increasing the importance of storage, grids, flexibility, and complementary technologies.

observations.period: 2025; regional distribution of renewable capacity growth

denominator.unit: GW of global renewable capacity additions in 2025

asia_share.unit: percent of new renewable capacity contributed by Asia

asia_additions.unit: GW of renewable capacity added in Asia

asia_growth.unit: percent annual growth in Asia's renewable capacity

africa_additions.unit: GW added in Africa, its highest capacity increase in the series

middle_east_growth.unit: percent annual renewable-capacity growth in the Middle East

observations.method: IRENA regional aggregation of country-level renewable capacity statistics and annual additions.
observations.uncertainty: Regional aggregates can hide very different country baselines, access conditions, grid constraints, financing environments, and off-grid activity.
observations.subgroup: Regions and countries with different energy-import exposure, public finance, grid capacity, energy poverty, industrial capabilities, and climate vulnerabilities.
observations.counterinterpretation: High regional concentration may change as financing, supply chains, policy, and grid investment diffuse; current shares are not fixed geopolitical outcomes.

observations.period: 2025; regional capacity stock and energy-security gap

denominator.unit: GW of global renewable capacity at end-2025

asia_stock.unit: GW of renewable capacity in Asia

europe_stock.unit: GW of renewable capacity in Europe

central_america_caribbean_stock.unit: GW of renewable capacity in Central America and the Caribbean

security_implication.value: uneven renewable capacity leaves low-share economies more vulnerable and underscores the need to increase renewable energy for energy security

off_grid_additions.unit: GW of off-grid electricity capacity added outside Eurasia, Europe, and North America

observations.method: IRENA comparison of regional renewable capacity stocks, off-grid additions, and energy-security implications.
observations.uncertainty: Capacity stock is not equivalent to energy access or energy security; it does not identify prices, outages, ownership, local pollution, or household-level incidence.
observations.subgroup: Low-capacity regions, energy-importing states, off-grid communities, utilities, public agencies, and households exposed to unreliable or expensive energy.
observations.counterinterpretation: Small capacity stocks can coexist with strong potential, distributed systems, imports, efficiency, or other forms of energy resilience; aggregate capacity is one component of security.

related_sources.claim: IRENA's release provides the 2025 capacity highlights and regional interpretation.
IRENA's yearbook page provides the historical capacity-statistics series and datasets.

record.boundary: This record adds a renewable-deployment route across capacity growth, technology concentration, regional inequality, off-grid systems, and energy security. It uses aggregate IRENA capacity statistics, not respondent-level energy histories, individual utility bills, plant-level operating records, causal forecasts, or proof that capacity growth produces equal affordability or security for every place.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official IRENA publication and 2025 capacity highlights reviewed for total capacity, annual additions, technology composition, regional distribution, capacity stocks, off-grid additions, and energy-security interpretation.

record.title: Cloud procurement becomes a public-capability and vendor-dependency decision
record.source_unit: World Bank, Enabling Cloud Procurement: A Guide for the Public Sector
record.geography: Public-sector ministries and agencies; comparative procurement and governance guidance drawing on public-cloud and digital-transformation cases

observations.period: 2026; public-sector digital and AI transformation through cloud services

denominator.unit: public-sector cloud-procurement system and layered technology stack

capability_route.value: AI services, data analytics, e-government systems, and disaster-recovery arrangements are increasingly delivered through cloud services rather than built as capital infrastructure

procurement_position.value: cloud procurement is on the critical path for digital and AI transformation because procurement and financial-management arrangements determine what services government can acquire and sustain

governance_model.value: the guide identifies a case for a centralized government cloud-procurement broker, standardized strategies, and whole-of-government framework agreements

continuity.value: cloud contracts need service-level expectations for availability, performance, data durability, incident response, and continuity rather than only one-off hardware delivery

observations.method: World Bank public-sector guide synthesizing cloud concepts, procurement policy, financial management, institutional arrangements, procurement routes, evaluation criteria, and real-life-inspired scenarios.
observations.uncertainty: The guide is practical policy guidance and does not estimate the causal effect of centralized procurement, cloud adoption, or AI services on public-service outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Ministries, agencies, procurement and finance teams, digital and AI offices, technical teams, implementing agencies, public-service users, cloud providers, integrators, and software vendors.
observations.counterinterpretation: Centralization can improve standards and bargaining power but can also concentrate decision-making, reduce local fit, or create a new single point of institutional failure; the guide does not prescribe one universal model.

observations.period: 2026; cloud procurement routes, supplier structure, and market participation

denominator.unit: procurement-route families discussed: direct contracting, indirect procurement, and framework or marketplace arrangements

supplier_access.value: open frameworks, supplier prequalification, and marketplaces are presented as ways to balance participation between large providers and smaller and medium-sized enterprises

competition.value: framework design and demand aggregation can simplify adoption and expand expertise, but must preserve competition, transparency, fairness, and fit-for-purpose evaluation

evaluation.value: evaluation should combine price with technical, security, privacy, interoperability, sustainability, and service considerations

market_power_mechanism.value: public procurement becomes a market-shaping institution that can either widen or narrow the provider ecosystem and distribute digital capability across firms

observations.method: Comparative procurement guidance covering direct and indirect routes, framework agreements, supplier accreditation, marketplaces, tender evaluation, SME participation, and sustainability criteria.
observations.uncertainty: The guide identifies design choices and risks but does not measure actual supplier concentration, SME entry, prices, or procurement performance across countries.
observations.subgroup: Cloud hyperscalers, local and regional providers, SMEs, independent software vendors, systems integrators, procurement officers, and governments seeking interoperable services.
observations.counterinterpretation: Large providers may offer stronger security, resilience, and technical capacity in some settings; maximizing the number of suppliers can add integration, oversight, and accountability costs.

observations.period: 2026; cloud risk, data control, portability, and public-service legitimacy

denominator.unit: public-sector cloud risk and exit-governance frame

lockin.value: without clear policy and institutional arrangements, procurement decisions can increase compliance risk, vendor lock-in, and resource risk

exit_controls.value: data portability, interoperability, non-proprietary services, multi-cloud options, and clear exit strategies with costs and timelines are emphasized as ways to reduce lock-in

public_trust.value: data residency, security, privacy, incident response, and continuity conditions connect cloud procurement to public trust and service reliability

accountability.value: the guide frames procurement, technical architecture, finance, security, and service assurance as linked accountability roles rather than isolated purchasing tasks

observations.method: Guide-based risk and contract analysis using cloud service layers, data governance, security and privacy criteria, interoperability, exit terms, service levels, and scenario-based procurement design.
observations.uncertainty: Recommended controls do not establish that a contract will be portable, that multi-cloud lowers total cost, or that security and privacy will be enforced in operation; outcomes require implementation audits.
observations.subgroup: Citizens using health, civil-registration, e-government, and smart-city services; data-protection officers; technical teams; vendors; auditors; and public managers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Cloud dependence can improve resilience, security, and access to expertise where governments lack in-house capacity; exit controls may be costly or technically limited for specialized services.

related_sources.claim: Official World Bank record, report number, date, project, abstract, and document metadata.
World Bank document API record containing the official PDF URL, abstract, report number, authors, and document identifier.

record.boundary: This record adds a procurement-to-public-capability mechanism linking cloud contracting to AI and data capacity, supplier market structure, lock-in, security, continuity, privacy, and public-service legitimacy. It is a World Bank implementation guide, not causal evidence that centralization, cloud adoption, or multi-cloud improves outcomes; all scenario benefits require live procurement and service audits.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official World Bank PDF, API metadata, cloud and AI transformation framing, centralized broker, procurement routes, SME participation, framework agreements, evaluation criteria, continuity, privacy, security, portability, exit, vendor lock-in, and public-service scenarios were reviewed.

boundary: This is a pinned historical snapshot for review. It does not harmonize units, establish independence, or prove a backtest result.
